• Choose a nice, straightforward distro to start out. Unless you want the maximum challenge and have a good deal of free time.

For beginners, any Ubuntu or any spin-off is solid. I personally dislike Unity, Ubuntu's desktop environment, but that's a matter of preference. You have a lot of possible choices when it comes to desktop interface. What follows are just my perceptions of each of these distros. It's subjective and I'm sure there are plenty of users that'll disagree with me. I'm also probably leaving something else

Here are some beginner options:

  1. Linux Mint - Ubuntu spin-off that has a slightly different interface. Don't use it but I've heard good things. Probably uses similar commands to Ubuntu (i.e., aptitude is package manager, I would imagine)

  2. Ubuntu

  3. Elementary OS - Ubuntu spin-off with a sexy interface. Haven't used it much but it looks solid and it should respond to the same commands that Ubuntu does.

  4. OpenSUSE Edit: See Kadivs' response to this comment.

Intermediate:

  1. Fedora

  2. Debian

  3. Slackware

Hard mode: 1. Gentoo - no install wizard, compiles everything from source. Would not recommend as your first Linux experience. Great documentation, though.

  1. Arch Linux - Deeply customizable, doesn't come with a GUI -- my personal favorite. Decent documentation (better than it used to be)

  2. Parabola - Arch Linux derivative that doesn't include any nonfree packages. Would not suggest for a first flirt with Linux.

  3. You don't need antivirus, so don't go paying for it. But don't go around executing random programs, shell scripts, or terminal commands that you're unfamiliar with. There are some pretty comprehensive lists of dangerous commands to run. Off the top of my head, never run 

rm -Rf /

Which deletes everything in the root directory recursively, including your files

:(){ :|:& };:

Which will create a program called ":" that replicates itself over and over consuming your CPU and your kernel's process table. (Newer Unices are better at handling this and it's not permanent--you just have to reboot, but still, avoid it.

dd if=/dev/null of=/dev/sda
or
dd if=/dev/random of=/dev/sda
dd if=/dev/urandom of=/dev/sda

The first command writes a bunch of emptiness to your HDD. The second two write junk data to your HDD. No bueno.

  • If you're dual booting, you should use a boot manager like GRUB (or Gummiboot, though it's a little harder to use) instead of the Windows boot manager. I know it's tempting, but the Windows boot manager is easier to fuck up and harder to fix. Plus it's not a very reliable way to boot into non-windows OSes.

  • Unless you want to do some specific tweaking, don't expect stellar battery life if you're using Linux on a laptop. In general, proprietary OSes have us beat in terms of battery life. I get about 9 hours on my Arch Linux laptop, while Windows only gets about 7, but I've done quite a lot of tweaking to get there.

  • Learn search-engine fu.

It really depends on fragmentation. Making a 100gb partition that has only 10gb used half as large is something entirely different than making a 100gb partition that has 98gb used 1 gb smaller, for example.
If your data is fragmented enough, you simply lose all parts that where in the locations once used up by the partition but not anymore due resizing. Before making a partition smaller, you should always defragment the partition, even if you have a file system that's supposed to be fragmentation resistant (better safe than sorry). If you have an encrypted partition, you really have problems as proper encryption fills the whole partition to equal parts. I have no idea if you can even resize one, frankly.
Making a partition larger is no problem, but still a risky thing, because any error during it and you can kiss your data goodbye (ok, undeleter tools should be able to, well, undelete many things in such a case).

ext4 won't fragment...it's just not how it works. It's not indexed and archived like NTFS or FAT which can fragment. Which is why you can't defrag an ext partition. But if you're worried, it's best to use linux utilities to modify ext4 partitions because they can check them for integrity.

NTFS and FAT are where you get the concern with fragmentation. Basic reason is that ext "scatters" files across the partition such that it's not that important "where" they are, while NTFS and FAT put them as close as possible to one another one-after-the-other. I don't even know of an ext defrag program.

I think you may have the way fragmentation works mixed up: The problem isn't that the files are scattered but that they're not "close" to one another in a fs like FAT or NTFS. Any even sort of decent partition utility will be copying all the relevant data from the partition to the location you want it in block sizes. If there's a problem, many utilities can also access that last block and write it again.

Give yourself time and find every excuse to do whatever-your-were-going-to-do-in-windows on your linux install. That's how you'll learn and become comfortable.

Use package managers. They make installation of programs so painless that the next-next-confirm-next-finish install that you're used to from windows will feel sloppy in comparison. The most commonly used managers are apt and yum. apt is used in Debian based distros (the most common ones are Debian, Ubuntu and Mint) while yum is used in Fedora based distros (such as Fedora and Red Hat). If you're unsure which package manager your distro is using, it's easily googlable.
A good place I get a lot of general and advanced linux information is the Arch Linux Wiki: https://wiki.archlinux.org/.
